description: ​We are a tech team working on creating health monitoring software for astronauts during space missions. Our project focuses on analyzing vital signs and using software/AI solution algorithms to monitor health risks and ensure astronaut safety.
summary:
Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to radiation, microgravity, isolation and
stress, while the distance from Earth makes real-time medical support impossible.
AstroPulse is a modular health and environmental monitoring software suite that
addresses this gap. It simulates astronaut telemetry (heart rate, blood oxygen, radiation,
bone density, stress, sleep), processes it in a backend core, keeps data safe through a
Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) layer during communication blackouts, and
presents everything on a real-time Heads-Up Display (HUD) for mission control.
An AI-assisted triage engine continuously assesses each crew member, flags risks such
as cardiovascular strain, space radiation exposure, hypoxia and neuro-ocular risk, and
issues recommendations with a confidence level. We chose this challenge because
astronaut health is the limiting factor for deep-space exploration, and because it
combines data engineering, networking, machine learning and UX in one end-to-end
system. AstroPulse meets the challenge requirements by delivering a working pipeline
from data generation to decision support that remains reliable under delayed and
disrupted links, and can be launched with a single click on any Windows machine.
details:
What it does and how it works

AstroPulse is a modular health and environmental monitoring suite for astronauts on deep-space missions. A telemetry simulator generates real-time vital signs (heart rate, blood oxygen, radiation exposure, bone density, stress, sleep) for each crew member. A FastAPI backend ingests, stores and serves this data. An offline Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) layer queues the data during communication blackouts and delivers it in order when the link returns. An AI triage engine classifies each astronaut as Nominal, Warning or Critical, names the likely risk (such as cardiovascular strain, space radiation exposure, hypoxia or neuro-ocular risk) and recommends an action with a confidence level. Everything appears on a real-time Heads-Up Display (HUD) with crew status cards, live charts and a medical alert feed.

Benefits

  • Early warning of health problems without waiting for Earth.
  • No data loss during delays or blackouts.
  • Raw numbers become clear, prioritized decisions.
  • Mission control sees every crew member and the link delay on one screen.
  • The whole system launches or stops with a single click.

Intended impact

AstroPulse supports safer long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where real-time medical support from the ground is not possible. It gives crews and flight surgeons a foundation for autonomous health monitoring that can later be connected to real sensors and flight data.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript (ES modules), JSX, CSS, HTML, PowerShell, SQL.
  • Backend and ML: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, SQLite.
  • Frontend: React, React DOM, Recharts, Vite, Tailwind CSS, PostCSS, Autoprefixer.
  • Data: hybrid real datasets and CSV files loaded with download_data.py, plus simulated telemetry, informed by NASA resources such as the Space Apps challenge page and the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).
  • Hardware: standard Windows laptops.

How it is creative

It combines telemetry, DTN, AI triage and a live HUD in one modular system designed for deep-space conditions. Most health dashboards assume a stable connection, while AstroPulse assumes delays and outages from the start. It also interprets the data instead of just displaying it, and its modular design lets teams swap the simulator for real sensors without changing the rest.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay (up to about 20 minutes one-way) and blackouts.
  • Reliable, ordered data delivery.
  • Clarity of the interface for quick decisions under pressure.
  • Modularity, so each component can be developed, tested and replaced independently.
  • Easy deployment through automation scripts.
  • The limits of simulated and public data, since real astronaut data is restricted. Validating with real flight data is the next step.
